title: How does ResearchAgent decide which article is worth buying?
abstract: Sourced guide to how ResearchAgent chooses a paid article: what the decision model scores, how a writer trust score weighs in, and the fixed policy checks behind each purchase.
body:
According to ResearchAgent documentation, ResearchAgent decides which article is worth buying in two steps: a decision model scores how useful each paid article would be, and policy code buys only what clears a threshold within the budget; no language model can spend. [1] [2]

For each missing fact, the model rates every candidate from its public title, abstract, topics and signed promises, never the paid text: how likely it is to fill the gap, whether it is original, and how credible its writer is. That value is multiplied by the writer's trust score, a number from 0 to 1, so trust can lower a score but never raise it. [1] [2]

Policy code, not the model, makes each purchase. It buys an article only when the value clears a fixed threshold for that model, the topics cover the question, the writer is in good standing, and the price fits both the per-article cap and the remaining budget. A new writer may get one labelled probe purchase of up to S$0.30 below that threshold. It buys at most one article per round, for up to three rounds, and stops once the requested facts are answered. [1] [3]

Author interpretation: the budget a person confirms in the plan step is the only spending authority. The language model plans searches and writes the answer, but it cannot sign a payment, raise the budget or tell policy which article to buy. After delivery, the passages are checked against the writer's signed promises, and a broken promise lowers that writer's trust in later decisions. Sources accessed 11 November 2026. [1] [3]
